newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal firms baulk at lengthy wage dispute.
newsitem.headline: German metal firms baulk at lengthy wage dispute.

text.p: German metal industry employers on Saturday conceded that they could not afford a long battle with workers over planned sick pay cuts and declared themselves willing to negotiate.

Werner Stumpfe, president of the Gesamtmetall employers' federation, said companies had to seek a compromise to prevent the kind of disruption caused by wage protests last week in which hundreds of thousands of workers took part.

"A really unusual situation would have to emerge before the German metals industry would be in a position to accept a battle with workers lasting several weeks," Stumpfe said at a meeting of employers in Essen.

Wild-cat protests occurred nationwide last week, causing lost production at steelworks and car assembly plants, after IG Metall union negotiators and Gesamtmetall failed to find a national agreement on how to cut labour costs.

Central to the dispute is a new law allowing a cut in workers' cherished sick payments from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, which no company has yet managed to implement because of furious union reaction.
On Saturday, around 5,000 metal workers took to the streets in the northern city of Kiel for a union rally.

IG Metall leader Klaus Zwickel reminded his audience of a two-month strike 40 years ago which had established German workers' rights to 100 percent sick pay and said entitlement could not be undermined in the future.

Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe insisted that wage costs had to be reduced but said there were alternatives to cutting 20 percent directly off sick pay, such as requiring employees to work an additional 1.4 hours for each sick day.
Separately Chancellor Helmut Kohl's spokesman on social issues, Rainer Eppelmann, said companies ought to be allowed to undercut wage contracts if emergency circumstances demanded it.

Eppelmann, who has criticised companies for trying to enforce sick pay cuts immediately, told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper that reductions in holiday or Christmas bonuses ought to be permissable in order to secure jobs. The interview was released ahead of publication.

The head of the DAG white collar workers' union Roland Issen threatened further protests over sick pay, telling the Magdeburger Volkstimme newspaper that employers could expect "massive conflict" if they did not drop the planned cuts.
